A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same solution-degeneracy study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison, with retained material identifiable despite relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v2.pdf reports original RNN training experiments across four tasks, including degeneracy measurements, OOD evaluations and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v3.pdf retains these original results and adds Lorenz 96 experiments, GRU tests, denser parameter sweeps and statistical controls.

M1.justification: The proposed framework, vanilla-RNN and µP equations, degeneracy metrics and regularization losses are retained. GRUs appear in an additional architecture-generalization test, without a newly proposed framework component or revised measurement algorithm.

E1.justification: V3 retains the four original neuroscience tasks and adds Lorenz 96 next-step prediction in 16, 24 and 32 dimensions (Appendix E). This substantially broadens coverage from tasks producing stable attractors to learning chaotic dynamics.

E2.justification: The existing SVCCA comparison is retained, and no competing degeneracy method is added or removed. Newly cited representation-comparison methods are contextual references; the GRU experiment tests the framework's applicability to another architecture.

E3.justification: The original task/training tables and temporal OOD procedures remain unchanged. V3 adds a Lorenz simulation and prediction protocol with 15,000 post-transient time points, time step 0.01 and MSE stopping threshold 0.0005, plus GRU channel sweeps, dense parameter sweeps and within-network null-control procedures. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: V3 adds final-loss comparability checks (Appendix C), within-network DSA and weight-permutation controls (F.3), GRU generalization tests (H), and denser feature-learning, width and rank-regularization sweeps (I). These address additional confounds and sensitivity questions; the earlier memory-demand, SVCCA, OOD and parameterization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions already report 50-network experiments and standard errors. V3 substantially extends statistical reporting with final-training-loss coefficients of variation across conditions (Tables 2–6) and 95% confidence intervals for within-network DSA null distributions (Table 7). No increase in the original repeated-run counts is established.

E6.justification: The matched main-result plots and Table 1 retain their values and trends. V3 adds Lorenz degeneracy results, a reported Lyapunov exponent of 12.58 ± 0.74 for the 16-dimensional condition, GRU and dense-sweep findings, and training-loss/null-distribution statistics (Figures 10–11, 13–14; Tables 2–7). These materially expand the reported evidence.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds the mathematical specification of Lorenz 96, including its differential equation, cyclic boundary conditions and initial-state distribution. The existing µP scaling equations and parameterization-equivalence derivation are retained; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the unified three-level framework, four controlling factors, and contrasting effects on dynamical and weight degeneracy. The Contravariance Principle claim and Table 1 conclusions remain unchanged; the added experiments principally support these retained claims.

C2.justification: V3 explains the dependence of DSA scale on its hyperparameters and interprets the new loss-variation and null controls as evidence against confounding explanations. It also makes the temporal-generalization scope of behavioral results more explicit. Existing overfitting interpretations, dynamics–behavior decoupling and limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies zero hidden-state initialization, γ = 1 for the width comparison, fixed within-task DSA hyperparameters and Lorenz data-generation details. Its checklist states that code and documentation accompany supplemental material, although actual availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. Earlier training and hardware disclosures remain.

R1.justification: V3 expands task motivation using attractor-memory, working-memory, central-pattern-generator and path-integration literature, and adds Lorenz and geometric-comparison references. Several introductory citations are replaced, but the central positioning around solution degeneracy and the Contravariance Principle is retained.

P1.justification: V3 revises task motivation, DSA explanations and feature-learning prose, nests the feature-learning intervention under Section 3.2.2, reorganizes appendix labels and adds a conference checklist. Author and acknowledgment text also changes. The overall narrative structure and most retained exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds substantial quantitative displays: Tables 2–7 for loss variability and null intervals, and Figures 10–11 and 13–14 for chaotic trajectories, Lorenz experiments, GRUs and dense sweeps. Retained plots largely preserve their content while undergoing relocation, resizing, renumbering and caption refinements.

improvement.justification: V2 did not directly quantify residual training-loss variation or establish within-network reference distances. V3 adds these controls and extends validation to chaotic dynamics, GRUs and denser parameter ranges (Appendices C, E, F.3, H and I). These additions substantially strengthen confidence that the central degeneracy findings reflect meaningful, robust differences between trained solutions. The GRU extension remains preliminary, but the overall empirical foundation is materially stronger.
